steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a computational social science paper showing that a group of suspended Twitter accounts, beyond those attributed to the Internet Research Agency, behaved like IRA accounts and influenced the 2016 US election discourse. Cover the background on social media, misinformation and foreign interference, the IRA data release, prior studies of IRA activity and its impact, the gap our study addresses, our findings, and the paper outline.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Social media in politics and the risks
- Misinformation, disinformation and foreign interference
- The IRA operation and Twitter's data release
- Prior work characterizing the IRA campaign
- Prior work on the IRA campaign's impact
- Gap: suspended accounts not flagged as IRA; our question and findings
- Paper organization

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Social media and politics
  - platforms prominent in shaping political events and social discussions
  - political campaigns worldwide rely on them to communicate and shape public opinion
  - debates about impact on society, risks
- Misinformation / foreign interference
  - platforms can foster informed discussion but susceptible to misinformation and disinformation campaigns
  - beyond politics: public health, e.g. anti-vaccine movements during COVID-19
  - evidence some governments exploit platforms to subvert domestic movements and interfere in foreign adversaries' elections
  - examples: 2017 French presidential election; Internet Research Agency (IRA: Russian company, online influence operations for Russian business and political interests) in 2016 US presidential election
- IRA and Twitter data
  - U.S. Special Counsel's report: IRA began Russian interference operations as early as 2009
  - social network campaigns to fuel and magnify political and social divisions in US
  - start of 2018: Twitter committed to Congress and public to give updates on investigation into foreign interference
  - October 2018: Twitter released all accounts and content tied to potential information operations found since 2016
  - more than three thousand IRA-affiliated accounts; more than 9 million tweets; earliest activity back to 2009
  - Twitter estimate: 9% of IRA tweets election-related
- Characterizing the IRA campaign
  - Badawy et al.: conservatives retweeted Russian trolls much more than liberals, produced 36 times more tweets; 5.7 million distinct users, September 16 - November 9, 2016; ~4.9% liberal and 6.2% conservative users were bots sharing troll content; troll content mostly conservative, pro-Trump
  - Howard et al.: targeted many US communities, esp. most extreme conservatives and those sensitive to race and immigration; fake accounts infiltrated liberal and conservative communities, incl. black activist communities, to exacerbate divisions and influence agenda
  - Stewart et al.: network science + volumetric analysis; trolls shared content to polarized information networks, likely accentuating disagreement and division
  - DiResta et al.: campaign designed to exploit societal fractures, blur reality and fiction, erode trust in media, information environment, government, each other, democracy
  - Zannettou et al.: IRA vs random users; IRA more likely to spread politics; multiple identities over account lifespan; deliberate efforts to grow followers
- Impact of the IRA campaign
  - Bail et al.: longitudinal survey of one thousand Republican and Democratic Twitter users, late 2017; trolls might have failed to sow discord, mostly interacted with already highly polarized
  - Grinberg et al.: fake news exposure in 2016 concentrated in small group, strong political partisans

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Social media platforms are more and more important in shaping political events and social discussions. Political campaigns all over the world rely heavily on social media platforms to communicate with the masses and to shape public opinion. But the rise of social media has also led to debates about their impact on society and the possible risks of using them.

Social media platforms can help communication and informed discussions, but they are also open to the spread of misinformation and disinformation campaigns. This problem is not only about politics, it also reaches sensitive areas like public health, for example the anti-vaccine movements during the COVID-19 pandemic. There is a lot of evidence that some governments actively exploit social media platforms to subvert domestic social movements and to interfere in the democratic elections of foreign adversaries. Examples of this kind of foreign intervention are the case of the 2017 French presidential election and the very significant interference by the Internet Research Agency (IRA: a Russian company engaged in online influence operations on behalf of Russian business and political interests) in the 2016 US presidential election.

The U.S. Special Counsel's report says that the Internet Research Agency started Russian interference operations as early as 2009. Their strategy was to create social network campaigns to fuel and magnify political and social divisions within the United States. At the beginning of 2018, Twitter committed to the United States Congress and the public that it would provide regular updates and information about its investigation into foreign interference in U.S. political conversations on Twitter. In October 2018, Twitter openly released all the accounts and related content associated with potential information operations that they had found on Twitter since 2016. This dataset has more than three thousand accounts affiliated with the IRA. It contains more than 9 million tweets, including the earliest Twitter activity of the accounts connected with these campaigns, which goes back to 2009. Twitter estimates that 9% of the tweets from IRA accounts were election-related.

After that, the number of works about the role of the IRA in the 2016 US political campaign and social debates increased. A. Badawy et al. found that conservatives retweeted Russian trolls significantly more often than liberals and produced 36 times more tweets. Out of the 5.7 million distinct users analyzed between September 16 and November 9, 2016, about 4.9% of liberal users and 6.2% of conservative users were automated accounts (bots) used to share troll content. Text analysis of the content shared by trolls shows that they had a mostly conservative, pro-Trump agenda. P. N. Howard et al. concluded that the Russian strategies targeted many communities in the United States, especially the most extreme conservatives and people with particular sensitivities to race and immigration. They found that the IRA used a variety of fake accounts to infiltrate political discussions in liberal and conservative communities, including black activist communities, to make social divisions worse and to influence the agenda. L. G. Stewart et al. combined network science and volumetric analysis and found that troll accounts shared content to polarized information networks, which likely accentuated disagreement and fostered division. These conclusions are in line with what R. DiResta et al. found, namely that the IRA campaign was designed to exploit societal fractures, blur the lines between reality and fiction, and erode trust in media entities and the information environment, in government, in each other, and in democracy itself. In their study on disinformation S. Zannettou et al. investigated the behavioral differences between IRA and random Twitter users. They found that IRA users are more likely to spread content related to politics. Also, the IRA used multiple identities during the lifespan of their accounts and made deliberate efforts to increase their impact on Twitter by increasing their number of followers.

- Impact of the IRA campaign
  - Bail et al.: longitudinal survey, one thousand Republican and Democratic users, late 2017; trolls may have failed to sow discord, mostly reached the already highly polarized
  - Grinberg et al.: fake news exposure in 2016 concentrated in small group of strong partisans
  - if IRA exposure similarly concentrated -> minimal impact on candidate preferences?
  - Eady et al.: over 1496 respondents + Twitter data; exposure concentrated among small fraction of self-identified Republicans; no significant relationship with attitudes, polarization, voting
- Gap and our findings
  - little attention to suspended accounts not flagged as IRA
  - "Twitter purge" May 2018; IRA only a smaller fraction of suspended accounts
  - did other suspended accounts also try to influence discourse / the 2016 election?
  - yes: consistent group similar to IRA in what they interact with and spread; Granger-causal influence on retweet activity of undecided users and weak supporters (polarization)
- Organization
  - Section 2 data and methods; Section 3 findings a) b) c); discussion and conclusion

Badawy et al. found that conservatives retweeted Russian trolls significantly more often than liberals and produced 36 times more tweets. Out of the 5.7 million distinct users analyzed between September 16 and November 9, 2016, about 4.9% of liberal users and 6.2% of conservative users were automated accounts (bots) used to share troll content. Text analysis of the content shared by trolls shows that they had a mostly conservative, pro-Trump agenda. P. N. Howard et al. concluded that the Russian strategies targeted many communities in the United States, especially the most extreme conservatives and people with particular sensitivities to race and immigration. They found that the IRA used a variety of fake accounts to infiltrate political discussions in liberal and conservative communities, including black activist communities, to make social divisions worse and to influence the agenda. L. G. Stewart et al. combined network science and volumetric analysis and found that troll accounts shared content to polarized information networks, which likely accentuated disagreement and fostered division. These conclusions are in line with what R. DiResta et al. found, namely that the IRA campaign was designed to exploit societal fractures, blur the lines between reality and fiction, and erode trust in media entities and the information environment, in government, in each other, and in democracy itself. In their study on disinformation S. Zannettou et al. investigated the behavioral differences between IRA and random Twitter users. They found that IRA users are more likely to spread content related to politics. Also, the IRA used multiple identities during the lifespan of their accounts and made deliberate efforts to increase their impact on Twitter by increasing their number of followers.

The studies above try to characterize the IRA campaign. To evaluate the impact of the IRA campaign on Twitter users, C. Bail et al. did a study with a longitudinal survey that describes the attitudes and online behaviors of one thousand Republican and Democratic Twitter users in late 2017. Their findings suggest that Russian trolls might have failed to sow discord because they mostly interacted with people who were already highly polarized. N. Grinberg et al. showed that exposure to fake news content during the 2016 elections was usually concentrated in a small group of users, especially those who identify themselves as strong political partisans. If exposure to posts from Russian foreign influence accounts during the 2016 US election was also concentrated like this, their impact on changing candidate preferences may have been minimal. To check this hypothesis, Eady et al. combined US longitudinal survey data from over 1496 respondents with Twitter data. They found that exposure to the Russian foreign influence campaign was heavily concentrated in a small fraction of users who identified themselves as Republicans. They also found no evidence of a significant relationship between exposure to the campaign and changes in attitudes, polarization, or voting behavior in the 2016 US election.

Prior research looked a lot at the influence of IRA accounts on individuals' voting intentions and Twitter discussions, but it gave limited attention to the broader set of suspended accounts that were not flagged as IRA. During the "Twitter purge" in May 2018, Twitter suspended many accounts, including ones unrelated to the IRA, and the IRA accounts were only a smaller fraction of this overall set.

All these accounts were suspended for violating Twitter rules, so this raises the question of whether, other than the IRA accounts, other accounts might have tried to influence Twitter discourse and more broadly the 2016 US election.

Our findings give evidence for this idea. A consistent group of suspended accounts is similar to the IRA accounts in terms of the information they interact with and spread to the broader Twitter community. We show that this group of suspended accounts did influence, in a Granger-causal manner, the retweet activity of undecided users and weak supporters, meaning people who are uncertain about their voting decisions, in terms of political polarization.

The paper is organized like this. Section 2 describes the data collection and analysis methods used in the study. Section 3 presents our findings, which include: a) the characterization of the users in our dataset based on the content they share; b) the use of the IRA ego network to identify a group of suspended users with similar behavioral patterns; and c) an evaluation of how this group of suspended accounts influences Twitter discourse, using Granger causality. The manuscript ends with a discussion and conclusion section that summarizes the key insights from our analysis.

At the beginning of 2018, Twitter committed to the United States Congress and the public to provide regular updates and information on their investigation into foreign interference in U.S. political conversations on Twitter. In October 2018, Twitter openly released all the accounts and related content associated with potential information operations they had found on Twitter since 2016. This dataset consists of more than three thousand accounts affiliated with the IRA. It contains more than 9 million tweets, including the earliest Twitter activity of the accounts connected with these campaigns, dating back to 2009. Twitter estimates that 9% of the tweets from IRA accounts were election-related.

Since then, the number of works focusing on the role the IRA played in the 2016 US political campaign and social debates has increased. A. Badawy et al. [16] found that conservatives retweeted Russian trolls significantly more often than liberals and produced 36 times more tweets. Among the 5.7 million distinct users analyzed between September 16 and November 9, 2016, about 4.9% and 6.2% of liberal and conservative users, respectively, were automated accounts (bots) used to share troll content. Text analysis of the content shared by trolls shows that they had a mostly conservative, pro-Trump agenda. P. N. Howard et al. [17] concluded that the Russian strategies targeted many communities within the United States, particularly the most extreme conservatives and those with particular sensitivities to race and immigration. They found that the IRA used a variety of fake accounts to infiltrate political discussions in liberal and conservative communities, including black activist communities, to exacerbate social divisions and influence the agenda. Combining network science and volumetric analysis, L. G. Stewart et al. found that troll accounts shared content to polarized information networks, likely accentuating disagreement and fostering division [18]. These conclusions align with the findings of R. DiResta et al. [19], who observed that the IRA campaign was designed to exploit societal fractures, blur the lines between reality and fiction, and erode trust in media entities and the information environment, in government, in each other, and in democracy itself. In their study on disinformation, S. Zannettou et al. [20] investigated the behavioral differences between IRA and random Twitter users. They found that IRA users have a higher tendency to disseminate content related to politics. In addition, the IRA employed multiple identities throughout the lifespan of their accounts and made deliberate efforts to amplify their impact on Twitter by increasing their number of followers.

The studies mentioned above aim to characterize the IRA campaign. To evaluate the impact of the IRA campaign on Twitter users, C. Bail et al. conducted a study using a longitudinal survey describing the attitudes and online behaviors of one thousand Republican and Democratic Twitter users in late 2017 [21]. Their findings suggest that Russian trolls might have failed to sow discord because they mostly interacted with those who were already highly polarized. In [22], N. Grinberg et al. showed that exposure to fake news content during the 2016 elections was typically concentrated among a small group of users, particularly those who identify themselves as strong political partisans. If exposure to social media posts from Russian foreign influence accounts during the 2016 US election was similarly concentrated, their impact on changing candidate preferences may have been minimal. To verify this hypothesis, Eady et al. [23] combined US longitudinal survey data from over 1496 respondents with Twitter data. They found that exposure to the Russian foreign influence campaign was heavily concentrated among a small fraction of users who identified themselves as Republicans. Moreover, they found no evidence of a significant relationship between exposure to the campaign and changes in attitudes, polarization, or voting behavior in the 2016 US election.

While prior research has extensively explored the influence of IRA accounts on individuals' voting intentions and Twitter discussions, it has paid limited attention to the broader set of suspended accounts not flagged as IRA. During the "Twitter purge" in May 2018, Twitter suspended numerous accounts, including those unrelated to the IRA [24,25], with IRA accounts making up only a smaller fraction of this overall set.

Since all these accounts were suspended for violating Twitter rules, this raises the question of whether, beyond IRA accounts, other accounts might have attempted to influence Twitter discourse and more broadly the 2016 US election.

Our findings provide evidence supporting this idea. A consistent group of suspended accounts is similar to IRA accounts in terms of the information they interact with and disseminate to the broader Twitter community. We demonstrate that this group of suspended accounts did influence, in a Granger-causal manner, the retweet activity of undecided users and weak supporters—individuals uncertain about their voting decisions—in terms of political polarization.

The paper is organized as follows: Section 2 outlines the data collection and analysis methods used throughout the study. In Section 3, we present our findings, which include: a) the characterization of users within our dataset based on the content they share; b) the use of the IRA ego network to identify a group of suspended users with similar behavioral patterns; and c) an evaluation of how this group of suspended accounts influences Twitter discourse, using Granger causality. The manuscript concludes with a discussion and conclusion section summarizing the key insights from our analysis.
